The child who keeps putting strange things in their mouth

Something dropped on the floor, a pellet from a flower bed, an object they've never seen before—a curious child tries to bring anything and everything to their mouth first. Parents are always on edge, worried their child might swallow something dangerous the moment they look away.

Putting things in the mouth is a natural way for a child to explore the world. The problem is they can't yet tell what's dangerous. So what's needed isn't a ban of 'don't eat that,' but a habit of judging for themselves and checking with a grown-up.

Curious about the plot of the child who puts everything in their mouth? Explore the lesson through the illustrations. Meet the key scenes of the story too. Read it with your child and talk about it together. We've gathered many stories about If It's Strange, Don't Eat It—Ptooey! covering preventing swallowing of foreign objects, children's safety education, not eating strange things, and more.

content.text:
Why the habit of judging for themselves matters

Parents can't always be right there watching. That's why it's important for a child to be able to stop and think, 'This looks strange, so I should ask first.' This habit becomes a reliable safety net that prevents accidents like swallowing foreign objects.

What matters isn't scaring them, but helping them understand why something is dangerous and teaching them the action of checking. One promise—to ask a grown-up first when something is strange—protects your child in a critical moment.

content.text:
Kongi's 'if it's strange, don't eat it' story

In "If It's Strange, Don't Eat It—Ptooey!", the little foodie Kongi spots a shiny red pellet in a park flower bed and tries to put it in his mouth. Just then Hori and Toto rush over and grab his hand, and the three of them run to Dad to show him.

Dad shares a story about how 'our mouth is a precious door' and teaches three promises. A little later, when Kongi sees a strange gray lump, he keeps the promise on his own and asks a grown-up. Now, whenever Kongi sees something strange, he keeps the three promises himself.

content.text:
Let's practice together at home

After reading, set your own family's safety promise. First, rather than the ban 'don't eat anything,' explain why it's dangerous through a story, like 'the mouth is a precious door.'

Second, make it a promise that when they see something strange, they ask a grown-up first, 'Can I eat this?' Third, look together for things you shouldn't eat inside and outside the home, practicing telling safe things from dangerous ones.

content.text:
Frequently asked questions

Q. What should I do about a child who puts everything in their mouth?

A. Gently set the promise to not eat strange things and to spit them out—ptooey. Sorting what's okay to eat from what isn't, like a game, helps your child be careful on their own.

Q. How should I react when they try to put a dangerous object in their mouth?

A. Rather than startling them greatly, calmly get them to stop and explain why it's not allowed. For a child who puts everything in their mouth, repeated promises and praise are the biggest help.

Q. When does the phase of bringing everything to the mouth out of curiosity pass?

A. The phase of checking everything with the mouth gradually fades as they grow. In the meantime, keeping small objects out of reach and watching over them safely is what matters most.
